source.title: Removing refusal in LLMs: Diff-in-means vs. Iterative Nullspace Projection

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes figure captions but not the plotted values from Figure 4; otherwise it is a complete study text.
record.tranche_reason: It applies diff-in-means directional ablation and activation addition, alongside other interventions, to five new chat models and evaluates refusal-related behavior and performance. The plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text.
record.gate_note: The text reports results for the project's interventions, but the numerical values in Figure 4 are not included. The text also says the P(α=1)=P sanity-check results are omitted; they are not recorded as findings. Results cited from Arditi et al. are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study reruns diff-in-means extraction on five of Arditi et al.'s chat models and compares it with INLP, a multi-direction erasure method. The question is whether refusal is one direction or several. Its own results bear on V1, because the first INLP direction matches diff-in-means and directional ablation removes refusal. They bear on V4, because the extra INLP directions add little. All evidence is prose describing Figure 4; no numbers are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with two corrections. The authors say nullspace projection does remove refusal but does not always beat directional ablation. The heaviest perplexity costs come from reflection (Gemma, Qwen), with nullspace projection costing more in Qwen and Yi. They conclude refusal is primarily mediated by one direction and that the vulnerability is genuinely low-dimensional.
record.recipe_differences: Uses diff-in-means and directional ablation with evaluations related to the original study, alongside INLP nullspace projection and classifier-weight ActAdd. Extraction uses residual-stream activations at prompt-final tokens; ablation/projection can be applied at different layer scopes. The prose results do not expose the comparison's numerical values.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported differences by model: Qwen is an exception to ActAdd comparability; reflection and nullspace projection show differing safety and perplexity outcomes across models. INLP is described as sensitive to classifier count and regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: INLP nullspace projection and α=2 reflection raise perplexity sharply in Gemma, Qwen and Yi. Reflection produces repeated text in Gemma.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-direction linear concept erasure of harmfulness costs more general capability than single-direction refusal ablation.

record.problems: The write-up calls results preliminary. Numerical values from Figure 4 are unavailable in the supplied text. The authors note small tested models (1.8B–8B), sensitivity to INLP hyperparameters, unaccounted composition effects across layers, and coarse substring matching for refusal. They also state that not all experimental settings are included.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. MMLU and ARC were evaluated according to the methods section, but the supplied text gives no readable results for them; Figure 4's plotted values are unavailable, so no separate metric rows can be extracted.

untested.parts: 'Other abilities largely kept' for diff-in-means ablation: MMLU, ARC and perplexity results for directional ablation are not reported in prose. No absolute rates of refusal removal or induction are given.
Affine, cone and rank-k descriptions. Only full INLP nullspace and reflection were tested; rank-k is listed as future work.

missing.what: Diff-in-means directional ablation results on refusal score and LlamaGuard unsafety versus baseline. The text implies refusal is removed and unsafe output rises above baseline.
missing.locator: Preliminary results · Refusal score and Safety score; Figure 4

missing.what: Diff-in-means ActAdd results versus baseline (refusal induction on harmless prompts, suppression on harmful prompts)
Perplexity, MMLU and ARC for directional ablation (the capability-preservation part of V1)

record.verdict_notes: This is a preliminary, non-peer-reviewed BlueDot project write-up. All results are prose descriptions of Figure 4, with no numbers, uncertainty or significance tests. INLP removes all linearly decodable harmful/harmless information, which differs from V4's refusal-specific affine or cone structure. So the V4 challenge applies only to that kind of subspace. The authors note INLP hyperparameters may not be optimal and that not all experimental settings are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not provide readable numerical results for diff-in-means directional ablation or all performance metrics, and does not establish that each component of V1 holds across all tested settings.
No conversion of activation ablation into a weight edit or released-model abliteration is reported.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or of training against its ablation is reported.
The study compares INLP and single-direction approaches but does not test an affine or cone description.
No separate encoding of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test is reported.
The study does not vary refusal training or its timing.

source_check.notes: Author and date are in the text: Elisabetta Rocchetti, BlueDot Impact, March 2026, code github.com/eliroc98/refusal_direction. All results are figure-only; the text gives no numbers. The safety-score paragraph contradicts itself on which way higher scores point ('higher always means better' vs '(meaning fewer genuinely unsafe responses)'), so method comparisons on LlamaGuard scores are ambiguous. The pack listed no [lN] ids, so labels are numbered l1 and l2 in listed order.

statements.correction: Nullspace projection generally removes refusal and does not always improve on directional ablation. Reflection (alpha=2) works in some cases, not consistently. R9: reflection fails for Qwen on LlamaGuard 2 safety score. Classifier-weight ActAdd performs well on harmless refusal; reflection does not work well. Authors: extra INLP directions 'add noise more than signal'. Authors attribute this to INLP capturing directions not related to refusal. Setup 'may not represent INLP at its best'. Rank-k subsets not tested (future work). All values figure-only; section titled 'Preliminary results'.
statements.problem: 'Give no refusal gain over the single direction' overstates the text: nullspace 'does not always improve' on directional ablation, which implies gains in some models. Reflection is never compared with the single direction. R9 is a Qwen LlamaGuard safety result, not a refusal-score result. The text points to the challenges label, but limits_scope fits better.

statements.correction: Nullspace projection 'does not always improve on directional ablation'. Reflection inconsistent. INLP 'sensitive to hyperparameters (number of classifiers, regularization)'. Rank-k restriction to fewer INLP directions listed as future work, not tested. Measures also include harmless-prompt refusal. Values in Figure 4 only.
statements.problem: 'No gain over the single direction' overstates the text: nullspace sometimes improves on directional ablation. The text says INLP is sensitive to hyperparameters, not 'to the classifier'. The study never isolates a second direction; it tests only the full INLP nullspace or reflection.
The statement is cut off in the pack, and the visible part makes no claim about this study.
